{{Short description|Zero divisors in a module}}
{{Other uses|Torsion (disambiguation)}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically in [[ring theory]], a '''torsion element''' is an element of a [[module (mathematics)|module]] that yields zero when multiplied by some [[non-zero-divisor]] of the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]]. The '''torsion submodule''' of a module is the [[submodule]] formed by the torsion elements (in cases when this is indeed a submodule, such as when the ring is an [[integral domain]]). A '''torsion module''' is a module consisting entirely of torsion elements. A module is [[torsion-free module|torsion-free]] if its only torsion element is the zero element.

This terminology is more commonly used for modules over a [[domain (ring theory)|domain]], that is, when the regular elements of the ring are all its nonzero elements.

This terminology applies to [[abelian group]]s (with "module" and "submodule" replaced by "[[group (mathematics)|group]]" and "[[subgroup]]"). This is just a special case of the more general situation, because abelian groups are modules over the ring of [[Integer#Algebraic_properties|integers]]. (In fact, this is the origin of the terminology, which was introduced for abelian groups before being generalized to modules.)

In the case of [[group (mathematics)|groups]] that are noncommutative, a ''torsion element'' is an element of finite [[order (group theory)|order]]. Contrary to the [[abelian group|commutative]] case, the torsion elements do not form a subgroup, in general.

== Definition ==
An element ''m'' of a [[module (algebra)|module]] ''M'' over a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'' is called a ''torsion element'' of the module if there exists a [[Regular element (ring theory)|regular element]] ''r'' of the ring (an element that is neither a left nor a right [[zero divisor]]) that annihilates ''m'', i.e., {{nowrap|1=''r''&thinsp;''m'' = 0.}}
In an [[integral domain]] (a [[commutative ring]] without zero divisors), every non-zero element is regular, so a torsion element of a module over an integral domain is one annihilated by a non-zero element of the integral domain. Some authors use this as the definition of a torsion element, but this definition does not work well over more general rings.

A module ''M'' over a ring ''R'' is called a ''torsion module'' if all its elements are torsion elements, and ''[[Torsion-free module|torsion-free]]'' if zero is the only torsion element.<ref>{{harvnb|Roman|2008|loc=p. 115, §4}}</ref> If the ring ''R'' is commutative then the set of all torsion elements forms a submodule of ''M'', called the ''torsion submodule'' of ''M'', sometimes denoted T(''M''). If ''R'' is not commutative, T(''M'') may or may not be a submodule. It is shown in {{harv|Lam|2007}} that ''R'' is a right [[Ore condition|Ore ring]] if and only if T(''M'') is a submodule of ''M'' for all right ''R''-modules. Since right [[Noetherian domain]]s are Ore, this covers the case when ''R'' is a right [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] [[domain (ring theory)|domain]] (which might not be commutative).

More generally, let ''M'' be a module over a ring ''R'' and ''S'' be a [[multiplicatively closed subset]] of ''R''. An element ''m'' of ''M'' is called an ''S''-torsion element if there exists an element ''s'' in ''S'' such that ''s'' annihilates ''m'', i.e., {{nowrap|1=''s''&thinsp;''m'' = 0.}} In particular, one can take for ''S'' the set of regular elements of the ring ''R'' and recover the definition above.

An element ''g'' of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] ''G'' is called a ''torsion element'' of the group if it has finite order, i.e., if there is a positive integer ''m'' such that ''g''<sup>''m''</sup> = ''e'', where ''e'' denotes the [[identity element]] of the group, and ''g''<sup>''m''</sup> denotes the product of ''m'' copies of ''g''. A group is called a ''[[torsion group|torsion (or periodic) group]]'' if all its elements are torsion elements, and a '''{{vanchor|torsion-free group}}''' if its only torsion element is the identity element. Any [[abelian group]] may be viewed as a module over the ring '''Z''' of integers, and in this case the two notions of torsion coincide.

== Examples ==

# Let ''M'' be a [[free module]] over any ring ''R''. Then it follows immediately from the definitions that ''M'' is torsion-free (if the ring ''R'' is not a domain then torsion is considered with respect to the set ''S'' of non-zero-divisors of ''R''). In particular, any [[free abelian group]] is torsion-free and any [[vector space]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''K'' is torsion-free when viewed as a module over ''K''. 
# By contrast with example 1, any [[finite group]] (abelian or not) is periodic and [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]]. [[Burnside's problem]], conversely, asks whether a finitely generated periodic group must be finite. The answer is "no" in general, even if the period is fixed.
# The torsion elements of the [[multiplicative group]] of a field are its [[root of unity|roots of unity]].
# In the [[modular group]], '''Γ''' obtained from the group SL(2, '''Z''') of 2×2 integer [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] with unit [[determinant]] by factoring out its [[center (group theory)|center]], any nontrivial torsion element either has order two and is [[conjugation (group theory)|conjugate]] to the element ''S'' or has order three and is conjugate to the element ''ST''. In this case, torsion elements do not form a subgroup, for example, ''S''{{Hair space}}·{{Hair space}}''ST'' = ''T'', which has infinite order.
# The abelian group '''Q'''/'''Z''', consisting of the [[rational number]]s modulo 1, is periodic, i.e. every element has finite order. Analogously, the module '''K'''(''t'')/'''K'''[''t''] over the ring ''R''&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''K'''[''t''] of [[polynomial]]s in one variable is pure torsion. Both these examples can be generalized as follows: if ''R'' is an integral domain and ''Q'' is its [[field of fractions]], then ''Q''/''R'' is a torsion ''R''-module.
# The [[torsion subgroup]] of ('''R'''/'''Z''', +) is ('''Q'''/'''Z''', +) while the groups ('''R''', +) and ('''Z''', +) are torsion-free.  The quotient of a [[torsion-free abelian group]] by a subgroup is torsion-free exactly when the subgroup is a [[pure subgroup]].
# Consider a [[linear operator]] ''L'' acting on a [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] vector space ''V'' over the field ''K''. If we view ''V'' as an ''K''[''L'']-module in the natural way, then (as a result of many things, either simply by finite-dimensionality or as a consequence of the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]]), ''V'' is a torsion ''K''[''L'']-module.

== Case of a principal ideal domain ==

Suppose that ''R'' is a (commutative) [[principal ideal domain]] and ''M'' is a [[finitely generated module|finitely generated ''R''-module]]. Then the [[structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain]] gives a detailed description of the module ''M'' up to [[isomorphism]]. In particular, it claims that

: <math>M \simeq F\oplus \mathrm T(M),</math>

where ''F'' is a free ''R''-module of finite [[free module|rank]] (depending only on ''M'') and T(''M'') is the torsion submodule of ''M''. As a [[corollary]], any finitely generated torsion-free module over ''R'' is free. This corollary ''does not'' hold for more general commutative domains, even for ''R''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''K''[''x'',''y''], the [[ring of polynomials]] in two variables.
For non-finitely generated modules, the above direct decomposition is not true. The torsion subgroup of an abelian group may not be a [[direct summand]] of it.

== Torsion and localization ==

Assume that ''R'' is a commutative domain and ''M'' is an ''R''-module. Let ''Q'' be the [[field of fractions]] of the ring ''R''. Then one can consider the ''Q''-module

: <math>M_Q = M \otimes_R Q,</math>

obtained from ''M'' by [[extension of scalars]]. Since ''Q'' is a field, a module over ''Q'' is a vector space, possibly infinite-dimensional. There is a canonical [[group homomorphism|homomorphism]] of abelian groups from ''M'' to ''M''<sub>''Q''</sub>, and the [[Kernel (algebra)|kernel]] of this homomorphism is precisely the torsion submodule T(''M''). More generally, if ''S'' is a multiplicatively closed subset of the ring ''R'', then we may consider [[localization of a module|localization]] of the ''R''-module ''M'',

: <math>M_S = M \otimes_R R_S,</math>

which is a module over the [[localization of a ring|localization]] ''R''<sub>''S''</sub>. There is a canonical map from ''M'' to ''M''<sub>''S''</sub>, whose kernel is precisely the ''S''-torsion submodule of ''M''.
Thus the torsion submodule of ''M'' can be interpreted as the set of the elements that "vanish in the localization". The same interpretation continues to hold in the non-commutative setting for rings satisfying the [[Ore condition]], or more generally for any [[Ore condition#Multiplicative sets|right denominator set]] ''S'' and right ''R''-module ''M''.

== Torsion in homological algebra ==

The concept of torsion plays an important role in [[homological algebra]]. If ''M'' and ''N'' are two modules over a commutative domain ''R'' (for example, two abelian groups, when ''R''&nbsp;=&nbsp;'''Z'''), [[Tor functor]]s yield a family of ''R''-modules Tor<sub>''i''&thinsp;</sub>(''M'',''N''). The ''S''-torsion of an ''R''-module ''M'' is canonically isomorphic to Tor<sup>''R''</sup><sub>1</sub>(''M'',&nbsp;''R''<sub>''S''</sub>/''R'') by the [[long exact sequence|exact sequence]] of Tor<sup>''R''</sup><sub>*</sub>: The [[short exact sequence]] <math>0\to R\to R_S \to R_S/R \to 0</math> of ''R''-modules yields an exact sequence <math>0\to\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M, R_S/R)\to M\to M_S</math>, and hence <math>\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(M, R_S/R)</math> is the kernel of the localisation map of ''M''. The symbol {{math|Tor}} denoting the [[functor]]s reflects this relation with the algebraic torsion.  This same result holds for non-commutative rings as well as long as the set ''S'' is a [[Ore condition#Multiplicative sets|right denominator set]].

== Abelian varieties ==
[[Image:Lattice torsion points.svg|right|thumb|300px|The 4-torsion subgroup of an elliptic curve over the complex numbers.]]
The torsion elements of an [[abelian variety]] are ''torsion points'' or, in an older terminology, ''division points''.  On [[elliptic curve]]s they may be computed in terms of [[division polynomials]].
